title: Boston pianists Sabie Lewis and Walter Johnson, when only black musicians played
summary: Whaley lists Boston pianists, says all clubs used black musicians until the First World War, and recalls his own 1912 jobs.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Well, now, we were talking about these two piano players. You said he could go to Boston and get all the piano players he wants.
Oh, yeah.
Well, what about New York? You were some more in Boston? Did you have some more of the guys from Boston?
Oh, yeah. I named Sabie Lewis.
Sabie Lewis.

Yeah, Sabie Lewis. He was a very great piano player. He used to play around all the places. Well, you see, up til the First World War, there was nothing but black musicians. White musicians didn't have a chance. All the clubs everywhere had black musicians in there. Walter Johnson was one of the greatest.
What did he play?
Walter Johnson, pianist.
Walter Johnson.
Yeah. He used to have a -- say, a dance and I would start the dance. Walter would come in --
You'd start playing in the band?
Sure.
I see.
I used to play with all the places. I had a job playing down on Dover and Washington Street in a place -- and this is right after I got out of high school.
And what year would that be about?
1912. I played around there, and I lived in Everett.
That's in Boston, around Boston.
Yeah.
Then you come up around there?

Oh, yeah. I was born in Boston. Church and Melrose. And there was another guy I had mentioned -- Henry Bachelor, piano player. See, we had a whole gang of piano players around there and they all were working, too. All had a government job, and we used to get jobs. I used to go down to the St. Jordan marsh there and go up in the man's office and sit down and talk with him, and get -- about a job. We'd talk over all the conditions and everything.
